summary.title: CAP theorem - Wikipedia
summary.one_liner: A distributed data store can guarantee at most two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance, and during a network partition you must choose between consistency and availability.
keywords: why can't a database have all three guarantees
takeaways: CAP states a distributed store can provide at most two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.
Partition tolerance is effectively required because no distributed system is safe from network failures, so the real choice during a partition is consistency or availability.
CAP consistency (all clients see the same data) differs from ACID consistency, and CAP availability differs from high availability in software architecture.
RDBMS systems lean toward consistency, BASE/NoSQL systems often lean toward availability, and some databases like MongoDB and Redis favor consistency during partitions.
PACELC extends CAP by adding the latency vs consistency trade-off when there is no partition.
summary.summary: The Wikipedia article explains the CAP theorem (also called Brewer's theorem), defining consistency, availability, and partition tolerance as used by Gilbert and Lynch, and describes the choice a system faces when a network partition occurs. It covers how databases are classified (CP, AP, and the claim that no NoSQL database is CA), the history from Brewer's 2000 conjecture to the 2002 formal proof and Brewer's 2012 clarification. It also summarizes the PACELC extension that adds a latency vs consistency trade-off when no partition exists. The page is a reference-style overview with citations rather than a hands-on tutorial.
